newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: SDLP's Hume takes tough stance on Sinn Fein pact.
newsitem.headline: SDLP's Hume takes tough stance on Sinn Fein pact.

text.p: Irish nationalist leader John Hume said on Sunday that his SDLP party would not consider a pact with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, to contest British elections this year until the IRA called a ceasefire. Hume, breaking weeks of silence, said in an article in the Irish Independent newspaper that Irish nationalists, who want to reunite the two Irelands, were under-represented in the British parliament becase of its first-past-the-post election system.

But he ruled out a pact with Sinn Fein to maximise the number of seats nationalists from the 40 percent Catholic minority could win until the Irish Republican Army called a ceasefire in their war against British rule over the province.
Sinn Fein is seeking a pact to undermine the power pro-British Protstant Unionists have in the British parliament after a general election due by May.
Unionists, who want the province to remain British, have nine seats in the Westminister assembly while the SDLP, the moderate mainstream voice of Irish nationalism, has four.

Hume also suggested that Sinn Fein, which polled 15 per cent in elections to a consultative forum last year, would have to end its official policy of boycotting the British parliament if it wanted to agree an electoral pact.

Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams won a British parliamentary seat in 1983 but refused to occupy it because it would have entailed allegiance to Britain, which he sees as the illegal colonial ruler of part of Ireland.

"If they (Sinn Fein) cannot jettison the policy of parliamentary abstention, is not the real logic of that position that they should abstain totally for an election to a parliament they do not recognise and in which they would not sit if elected?" Hume wrote. He said formal discussions on joint electoral strategy could take place only if the IRA ended a guerrilla campaign against British rule it launched last February after a 17-month truce.

"In circumstances of a complete end to violence, I believe that we can discuss all these issues reasonably and logically and work to end the misrepresentation of constituencies by Unionist MP"s." Hume said.

Senior members of the SDLP are openly against any deal with Sinn Fein because of the IRA's violence, which has dealt a severe blow to efforts to forge a negotiated settlement between pro-British Protestants and pro-Irish Catholics.
Hume, in poor health in recent years, has also declined to confirm or deny whether he will stand for re-election to his Foyle power base around Northern Ireland's second city, Londonderry.
Last week he dismissed as fanciful reports that he would stand for election as Irish President, a largely figurehead role, if Mary Robinson decides against re-election this year.

Under the Irish constitution anyone from Northern Ireland can stand for election in the Irish republic. Hume's name is one of several being considered by Irish political parties to replace Robinson if she stands down, political sources said.
